text: Over the past few months, we’ve seen a resurgence of always-on agents. Always-on agents are stateful and proactive, meaning they manage context across sessions and take actions without direct supervision. Underneath, they run on the same core loop as other agents. The difference is the surrounding architecture, which is built from primitives that control when the agents wake up, what carries over between runs, and how their work reaches the user. The resurgence is largely due to recent model advancements, which have made always-on agents more practical to run. First, the latest models have better judgment: they’re more reliable at understanding user intent and knowing when to check in. Second, intelligence is becoming cheaper, with long-horizon tasks benefiting the most. For example, on one long-horizon coding benchmark , Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5, compared with 40% less on typical workloads. Customers have started to ask us how to integrate this type of experience into their own products. Some companies want to make their existing agents more proactive, while others are looking to build them from the ground up. This post breaks down the primitives behind always-on agents and walks through how they fit together. An always-on agent is not actually “always on.” This is just a description of the user experience. In reality, the agent spends most of its time asleep, waking up periodically to do work. Each stretch of work is called a run : the agent receives an event, completes its task, and then saves information about what happened. A run works inside a session , which is the transcript of messages and tool calls. Once the run is finished, the agent goes back to sleep, and the cycle repeats indefinitely. The surrounding architecture of an always-on agent has five core primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox. Let’s take a look at each. Most AI agents only run when the user sends a message. In contrast, always-on agents can be triggered by many types of events, including webhooks, scheduled tasks, and background jobs. One tempting approach is to have each event source call the agent directly, but that has a few failure modes. For example, two events arriving at the same time can start competing runs, and a crash can lose an event entirely. This is where the event inbox comes in. Instead of calling the agent, every source sends an event to an inbox, where a worker picks it up. The simplest version has three components: The inbox should track the status of each event, and events can be deduplicated based on unique identifiers from the source. A relational database works well for the inbox, with every event appended as a new row. We recommend starting with one inbox per user, but you can split this further if you need more parallelism. When a new event comes in, the handler writes the event to the inbox and wakes the worker. The worker reads whatever is pending and starts a run. Events that continue earlier work, such as a reply from the user, resume an existing session, while everything else starts a new session. From there, the worker passes the events to the agent loop, waits for the run to finish, and marks the corresponding events as done. The implementation details can get tricky, so here are a few best practices: Together with the event inbox, timers let always-on agents be proactive. Timers generally fall into one of two categories: follow-ups or schedules. A follow-up is a deadline that the agent sets for itself, such as checking in on a reply. A schedule, on the other hand, is a recurring task that happens on a known cadence, such as a daily newsletter. Timers live in their own durable store, usually another database table, separate from the inbox. The inbox should only hold events that are ready to be worked on. A follow-up and a schedule can share a similar schema, but a schedule needs to track its recurrence as well. A timer doesn’t initiate a run on its own. Instead, a scheduler, usually a background service, polls the store at a fixed interval and fires anything that’s due. On each pass, the scheduler: For the scheduler, you can either build your own service or use a durable execution engine. Always-on agents work across many disjointed runs and rely on memory to maintain continuity. Similar to the event inbox and timers, memory should have its own store. In our products, such as Claude Code’s auto memory and the Messages API’s memory tool , this is implemented as a directory of files. For an always-on agent, the directories should map to durable storage, usually a database or an object store. This way memories outlive the worker. As a rule of thumb, memory should only hold what the agent can’t look up again. If something already lives in another system, such as an issue tracker, you should save a pointer instead. You can also add dreaming, which reviews past sessions to curate memories. Dreaming can replace outdated entries and find patterns that only show up across many runs. If you’re interested in learning more, our post on agent memory covers this in more detail. Before doing any work, the agent loads the system prompt, tool definitions, and memory files. This initial context “overhead” is included in every run, so we recommend keeping it lean and using prompt caching to lower costs. A new session starts only with this context overhead and the events that triggered the run. An existing session, on the other hand, brings back the messages and tool calls from its earlier runs. If a session becomes too long, you can either compact the older messages or start a new session. Both approaches lose detail, so anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory along the way. Permissions are where always-on agents carry the most risk. A run holds the user’s access and, by design, operates unattended. For each tool call, the agent needs to decide whether to proceed on its own, block it, or wait for approval. The components for permissions are the same ones other agents use: With most AI agents, the response is streamed to the user as it’s generated, so they can follow along as Claude reasons through the problem, calls tools, and writes its answer. Always-on agents, on the other hand, do most of their work in the background. The user gets the outcome and a few details, rather than the entire step-by-step breakdown. A run can end in one of three ways: Most always-on agents can get by with a “send” tool that delivers the message directly to the user. You only need a formal outbox when you want to pace your agent’s messages or allow your agent to recover from errors. The outbox is a separate table of outgoing messages, analogous to the event inbox. There’s also a dispatcher, usually a background service, that’s analogous to the worker. The dispatcher reads the pending messages, decides what to deliver, and sends those to the user. A request from a deferred tool call can either go through the outbox or be shown directly in the interface. Beyond delivery, it’s important to tune how many messages the agent sends. An agent that sends too many becomes noisy, while an agent that doesn’t send enough misses things that the user needs to know. We recommend building evals to find the right balance. In practice, it’s better for the agent to start quiet and then earn more of the user’s attention over time. Here is how the five primitives fit together: Every run starts with an event from the inbox, whether it’s a user message, a webhook, or a timer. When the worker picks up an event, it kicks off a run and wakes the agent in a new or existing session. The agent reads its memory to get a baseline, works within its permissions to take actions, and then updates its memory with anything it has learned. Once the run is finished, the agent pushes a row to the outbox, and the dispatcher delivers the message to the user. Together, these form a cycle. A run can set a timer that wakes the agent again later, and when the user replies to a message, their answer comes back as an event in the inbox. Each run is brief, but the cycle keeps going indefinitely, and that’s what makes the agent feel like it’s always on. Written by William Hu.
